items.title: I Mathematically CALCULATED the worth of Codex & Claude Code PLANS ($200=$4900?!)
items.summary:
Thank you to TestSprite for sponsoring this video: https://www.testsprite.com/?via=aicodingki-dw
Github repo for TestSprite: https://github.com/TestSprite/testsprite-cli
checkout my second channel AISeeKing for more cool ai stuff: https://www.youtube.com/@AISeeKing

In this video, I compare Codex, Claude Code, and GLM coding subscriptions based on their models, usage limits, apps, and API-equivalent value. I also explain why Codex is currently my recommendation for most developers, why I still prefer Fable 5.1 for certain coding tasks, and why the affordable GLM Coding Plan deserves a closer look.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Codex offers access to GPT-6 Astra alongside Sol, Terra, Luna, and agent-based features such as Ultra mode.
💰 Based on an exploratory sample, Codex’s subscriptions could represent substantial API-equivalent value, although the projections are not guaranteed monthly allowances.

So, I still like Fable 5.1 more than GPT-6 Astra for a lot of coding tasks. But if you ask me which subscription I would recommend right now, I would probably tell you to get Codex. And if your budget is smaller, GLM deserves a look as well. The usage limits in the actual apps make a big difference here. I also tested how much API priced usage these subscriptions could represent because I wanted to understand what I'm getting for 20, $100, or $200 a month. So, let's talk about the models, the plans, and what I found. I'll keep the calculations simple. Let's get right into it. Before we dive in, let me tell you something. Boris Journey built Claude code and he said something that stuck with me. He doesn't write the prompts anymore. The loop does. His job is to write the loop. A loop acts, observes a real signal, decides what to do next, and repeats until a goal actually holds. Five blocks: trigger, goal, the work, memory, and verification, the feedback gate. The one block allowed to say no, not done yet. Everyone tunes the model and the prompt. Almost nobody builds this block. And in 2026, your loop is only as good as its feedback gate. Here's what that cost me. I had a loop running for 2 days, test screen every single iteration. I came back to it proud of myself, opened the app, and the whole checkout flow was dead button, did nothing, no error, just dead. The agent had been running unit tests against its own mocks the entire time. Green on its own machine, reporting done on something no real user could actually use. A green run on the agent's own machine proves nothing. So, the question I got stuck on is what's the one signal that actually closes the loop? And it's the boring answer, the deployed thing behaving for a real user. That's the block I tell you to obsess over. The verifier I use is open source, the TestSprite CLI. The agent calls it mid-build and it drives the live app like a real user would, not mocks. The actual deployed thing, when it broke that checkout flow again, it didn't just say failed. It handed back a screenshot of exactly what the user would have seen. The dead button, frozen, the agent read. That patched it, reran. I wasn't in the loop for any of it. That's what a closed loop actually feels like. Not a bigger brain, a stricter referee. The model isn't your bottleneck anymore. The loop is. And the loop is only as good as what's allowed to tell it no. If you want to start using it, then the installation process is very simple. You'll need Node 20.19, 22.13, or 24 and up. Install with npm install g @testbright/testbright-cli. Grab your API key from the dashboard under settings, API keys, copy it. It only shows once. Run TestBright setup, paste your key in, then confirm everything's connected with TestBright auth status. That's it, you're ready to go. So, when you design your next one, don't start with the model. Start with the verifier, for me that's TestBright, open source Apache 2.0, links below. Now, Codex has a free allowance, although I wouldn't expect it to carry a heavy coding workflow. The paid plans I'm comparing are ChatGPT Plus at $20 a month, Pro 5X at $100, and Pro 20X at $200. Astro is rolling out to B Plus as well, so you don't have to start at $100 just to access the model. You also have Soul, Terra, and Luna for other workloads. There's ultra mode, which can delegate parts of a task to additional agents, although the options you see depend on your plan and rollout. Personally, I think Astro is close enough to Fable that Codex's current allowance makes it a better deal for most people. When I'm building something, I want enough room to make the first version, ask for changes, and work through the bugs. Now, for the value calculation, I priced the recorded input, cached input, and output at the corresponding API rates. API equivalent value means what that token activity would cost through the API. It doesn't mean the subscription deposits that much money into an API account, or that the API would produce exactly the same results. I tested the $200 Codex Pro 20X plan. During about 43 minutes of research and development work, the weekly meter moved from 0 to 3%. I audited the recorded activity, including known work and other local tasks, and calculated about $34 of API equivalent usage. For an illustrative unvalidated projection, I divided that value by the three percentage points, extended it to a full weekly allowance, and converted it into a 30-day estimate. I then scaled down for the cheaper plans using the advertised usage ratios. I didn't test those cheaper Codex tiers directly. If that relationship holds and I use the full allowance every week, the scenario comes to roughly $240 of API equivalent usage for the $20 plus plan, $120 for the $100 pro plan, and $4900 pro plan. I tried to check that conversion with another 20 Astra requests worth about $35 at API prices, and the weekly meter initially didn't move. It increased later, but other work had continued, so I couldn't assign that increase just to the test. Small rounded meter readings and uncertain update timing make the conversion unreliable. So, I measured the activity, but I haven't established a fixed monthly dollar allowance. Treat those figures as what the first sample would imply, rather than a promise of what every account delivers. OpenAI has also been giving eligible users banked resets. That's a saved one-time refill you can use later before it expires. A full reset refreshes your 5-hour and weekly Codex limits, and changes the weekly reset date. You can check for those in the usage settings. They're promotional, so availability varies, and future resets aren't guaranteed. I didn't use banked resets or purchased credits in these tests, so the calculations don't depend on getting those bonuses. But having a reset available when you run out is pretty useful for sure. The desktop app is another big reason like Codex. It can generate images with OpenAI's GPT image model while building your application. So, if you want a custom illustration for a landing page or character assets for a game, you can ask for them in the same task. That makes the result feel much more complete. Fable might give me a layout I prefer, but I still have to think about where the visual assets are coming from. Codex makes that part convenient, although generating images also uses your allowance. Its browser and computer use are pretty great, too. It can open your app in the built-in browser, click through it, inspect a problem, and check a fix. You can also use that browser for research, for a form that isn't submitting. I want the agent to actually try it and see what happens. Claude Code has browser tools as well, including in its desktop app. I just prefer how the Codex workflow comes together. And there's a fast mode for supported models with higher credit consumption, if faster responses are worth that trade-off to you. Outside coding, I prefer ChatGPT's chat interface, too, including on mobile. So, that subscription gives me something I like using away from my projects, as well. My concern with Codex is how often the usage rules and offers change. One moment the plan feels extremely generous, then the limits change, and another promotion comes along. I like how actively the team improves the app, and I think they've been responsive to feedback, but I would like the subscription to become more predictable. Anyway, now let's come to Claude Code. Claude Pro is $20 a month, Max 5X is $100, and Max 20X is $200. Claude has free chat, but that doesn't include a Claude Code allowance. Pro includes Opus and Sonnet usage, while Fable 5.1 requires additional paid credits. Max includes Fable, but only up to half of your weekly allowance can go toward Fable models. It uses that shared allowance faster, and continuing past the Fable limit costs extra. I ran code review, data analysis, and system design tasks. about 13 cents of API equivalent activity accompanied a four percentage point increase in the five-hour meter. Scaling that small sample gives roughly 3.35 of API equivalent usage per full pro session allowance. For a monthly scenario, I assumed one full five-hour allowance per day for 30 days. That gives about $101 for pro, $503 for max 5x, and 2013 tasks for max 20x. The max numbers are calculated from the advertised session ratios. I only tested pro. That schedule requires enough weekly capacity, which I couldn't establish because the weekly display stayed unchanged. So, these aren't measured monthly limits, and I can't use them to claim Codex delivers a specific multiple of Claude's value. The models and workloads differ, and Codex's calculation uses a weekly allowance, while Claude's uses an assumed daily schedule. What I can tell you from my broader experience is that I still prefer Fable 5.1 for a lot of front-end work and complex debugging. It's my favorite model out of his options. The subscription is what I find harder to recommend. If I'm paying $100 or $200, Fable is the model I want to use, and its allowance doesn't feel comparable to the room I currently get with Astra. Opus and Sonnet are useful, but personally, they aren't enough of a reason to recommend spending that much right now. Claude's desktop app also feels pretty sub par to me in terms of the overall experience and reliability. The CLI is a different story. I still prefer Claude Code's terminal experience over Codex's, so somebody who works mostly in the terminal has a stronger reason to choose it. Now, there's another part of the value calculation that matters when you're working on the same project, and that's caching. The model can reuse matching context from earlier requests at a lower input cost. My samples already had a lot of that. About 94% of Astra's input and 79% of Sonnet's input came from cache. Staying on a project can help with reuse, but it doesn't guarantee every request matches or that the cash lasts all month. I also calculated a hypothetical 98% reuse scenario. If the included allowance responds proportionally to those API cost savings, it could support about 25% more processed tokens for the Codex workload and 9.3% more for the Claude workload. I modeled those gains, I didn't measure them over a month. Claude sample spent most of its API value on output, which input caching doesn't discount. That's why the modeled gain was smaller. It doesn't mean Claude's caching is inherently worse. For scale, the $200 Codex scenario moves from about 2.8 billion to 3.6 billion processed tokens. The $200 Claude scenario moves from about 466 million to 510 million. Those totals include repeated cached context and inherit all the earlier assumptions. They aren't billions of tokens of new code or a comparison of completed work. The API dollar estimates stay the same in that caching scenario. Each unit of work becomes cheaper, so the same assumed allowance fits more of it, increasing both the token volume and the dollar value would count the savings twice. How much you actually use matters, too. Use half the assumed allowance and the projected value halves, while the subscription still costs the same. On both providers, the $100 tier advertises five times the base usage for five times the price. The $200 tier advertises 20 times for 10 times the price, giving twice the advertised allowance per dollar if you need it. Those multipliers don't establish identical weekly capacity for every model. Now, let's talk a bit about GLM because this is where the smaller budget option gets interesting. The GLM coding plan standard monthly prices are $18, $80, and $168 with discounted offers available as well. Check the billing period when comparing prices. Zcode itself is free to download and new users can try GLM through trial quota. The $18 plan stands out to me for how much usage it offers. I wouldn't call it numerically equivalent to a $100 Codex plan because the models and quota systems differ, but I think it deserves to be considered alongside much more expensive options, especially if running out of allowance is your main problem. GLM also works really well with C code. It has browser automation to interact with an interface and check its work, and it can keep working toward a goal on longer tasks. I think the combination is capable across a lot of everyday coding work with enough room to build something and keep improving it. I haven't calculated an API equivalent dollar figure for GLM in this research. My recommendation here is based on its practical value and generous limits. If your budget is tight, it's a really good option to consider before jumping to $100 or $200. So, between Claude Code and Codex, I would currently recommend Codex to most people, particularly if you want a desktop app. Astra is strong. The current allowance feels better to me, and the image generation and browser workflow add a lot. That's my overall experience, separate from the exploratory dollar calculations. If Fable consistently does better on your important tasks, and you prefer Claude Code's CLI, Max can still make sense. And if you mainly want affordable coding capacity, try Z code and look at the 18 GLM plan. I would start with the smallest plan that handles my work. The larger tiers can look impressive in a calculation, but I would upgrade when I'm actually using up the smaller allowance. Paying for capacity I don't need doesn't help me finish anything. Overall, it's pretty cool.
